title: The saint-soldier
hookLine: the Khalsa ideal holds prayer and courage together in one person
tomorrow: Two flags at the Akal Takht

cards: At dawn, someone sits cross-legged, eyes closed, lips moving with a prayer. Later that day, someone stands between a bully and the kid being bullied, and doesn't step aside.
It's easy to file them in different drawers: the quiet one and the brave one, the monk and the firefighter.
The Sikh tradition keeps asking a stubborn question: why not the same person, someone who prays at dawn and, when it's needed, stands in the doorway? Today: the saint-soldier.

teach.b: Sant is a saint, a holy person whose mind rests in God. Sipahi is a soldier, a Persian word; the English sepoy comes from it. Together, sant sipahi is a phrase Sikhs often use for the Khalsa ideal.
It has a history. The first Gurus were teachers of the Name, poets and farmers.
Then, in 1606, the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, was executed in Lahore by the Mughal authorities. His son, Guru Hargobind, became the sixth Guru as a boy, and tradition says he put on two swords.
One he called miri, worldly responsibility. The other, piri, spiritual authority. Both at once.

Nearly a century later, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699 and gave the idea its fullest form: keep the daily prayers and the discipline of the Name, and stand ready to protect the weak and resist injustice.
The saint comes first, in the phrase and in the life. The daily prayers aren't a warm-up before the real work; they're the root, and courage grows out of them.
Without the saint, the soldier is only force. Without the soldier, the saint may watch injustice and do nothing. Sikhs don't read this as a call to go looking for fights.
A saint-soldier may never touch a weapon beyond the small kirpan. Their courage looks like telling the truth in a meeting, or refusing to laugh along. The prayer steadies them.

how: Sikhs describe the Khalsa ideal as sant sipahi, saint-soldier: an initiated Sikh keeps the daily prayers and discipline and also stands ready to defend the weak and resist injustice.

o: one person who holds both prayer and courage
a soldier who guards a gurdwara's door
a saint who has left behind all fighting

games.q: what's inside the idea — tap the pairs.
p: a saint, mind resting in God

s: the saint-soldier ideal means looking for fights
a saint-soldier may never carry more than the small kirpan; the courage is telling the truth, standing beside someone.
Guru Hargobind is said to have worn two swords
miri and piri: worldly responsibility and spiritual authority, worn at once.
the English word sepoy comes from sipahi
sipahi is a Persian word for soldier.

games.q: 1606. your father, the fifth Guru, has just been executed. you are the new Guru, still a boy. what do you put on?
o: a monk's robe, and withdraw from the world.
two swords, one for worldly and one for spiritual authority.
nothing new; everything stays as before.
games.why: tradition says Guru Hargobind wore two swords, miri and piri. prayer and responsibility, held together.

practice: First the saint: settle, and if you pray, use a line you know; if not, rest your mind on something good and true for a few breaths.
Then the soldier: from that steady place, bring to mind one small brave thing waiting for you, a hard conversation, a truth to tell, someone to stand beside. Don't do it yet; just decide you will.

wordCard.voice: Sant sipahi. The saint-soldier: prayer and courage held together in one person, with the saint first.

carryVoice: Your line: saint and soldier. The prayer is the root; the courage grows from it. That's day two hundred seventy-four.
